Company contact details are also provided.

structure.title: Credit Solutions that
structure.summary: Shriram Finance Limited, established in 1979, is a leading Indian NBFC that has transformed the credit ecosystem by expanding financial access, enabling economic growth, and empowering millions with tailored lending solutions. It supports customers across generations with strong digital capabilities and deep customer understanding, while remaining committed to reaching the unbanked and underserved through agile, innovative, and timely financial solutions. The company has 46 years of legacy, is one of India's largest retail asset-backed NBFCs, and reports assets under management of Rs. 263,190 crores as of March 31, 2025.

nodes.title: GLOBAL ECONOMIC OVERVIEW
nodes.summary: The text provides a global economic overview for 2024, noting 3.2% growth, below the historical average, due to policy tightening, geopolitical instability, and sector challenges. nodes.title: INDIAN ECONOMIC OVERVIEW
nodes.summary: The text provides an overview of India's economic performance in FY 2024-25, highlighting a 6.5% GDP growth driven by infrastructure investment, rural demand, and services expansion. The RBI cut the repo rate by 50 bps to 5.50% and reduced CRR by 100 bps, injecting INR 2.5 trillion liquidity. The Union Budget FY 2025-26 raised capital expenditure to INR 11.21 lakh crores and trimmed the fiscal deficit target to 4.9%, aided by the RBI's record dividend. Consumption revival measures include rural schemes, DBTs, and tax relief. The outlook projects 6.3-6.8% growth in FY 2025-26, supported by reforms, digital evolution, and initiatives like Make in India and PLI.

nodes.title: INDIAN FINANCIAL SERVICES SECTOR OVERVIEW

Challenges include unsecured lending, credit card delinquencies among youth, and pressure on net interest margins, yet the sector remains poised for growth with regulatory support and digital infrastructure.

nodes.title: NBFC Sector Outlook: Growth, Regulation, Technology, and Opportunities

Regulatory and market dynamics include RBI's scale-based regulations, funding diversification, and competition from banks and fintechs. nodes.title: Commercial Vehicle (CV)
nodes.summary: The text covers four Indian automotive sectors in FY 2024-25. Commercial vehicles show mixed trends: retail sales up 8.22% YoY, wholesale down 3.2%, M&HCVs expected to peak at ~550,000 units, LCVs stagnating, and buses growing 8-11%. The market is estimated at USD 51.09 billion with a 5.36% CAGR, driven by infrastructure, replacement demand, and electrification, but challenged by costs and policy fluctuations. Passenger vehicles hit an all-time high of ~43 lakh units (2% growth), led by SUVs, with the market projected to reach USD 300 billion by 2026, aided by rising incomes and EV adoption despite infrastructure and affordability barriers. Two-wheelers grew over 9%, with ICE holding 88% share and EVs surging 33%, expected to grow at a 21% CAGR; challenges include charging infrastructure and competition. Tractors saw a 5% YoY rebound from April-December and 11.31% growth in January 2025, supported by monsoons and mechanisation, with the market projected to grow at 6.70% CAGR from USD 7.42 million in 2023 to USD 11.68 million by 2032, led by northern regions.

nodes.title: Indian Auto Sector FY25: PV and 2W Market Overview
nodes.summary: The page covers India's passenger vehicle (PV) and two-wheeler (2W) markets in FY25. The market is projected to reach USD 300 billion by 2026, with EVs as a key growth catalyst despite infrastructure and affordability challenges; digitalization is transforming sales. 2Ws grew over 9%, with ICE holding 88% share and EV retail sales up 33%, forecast at 21% CAGR through FY29. Premium features, eco-friendly mobility, and government incentives drive growth, though infrastructure gaps and competition persist. Future growth is expected at 2-4%, steered by smart connectivity, safety, and performance innovations.

nodes.title: Gold Loan

Continuous investments support technology upgrades, IT security, training, and awareness. The Company follows a Zero-Trust Security model. New initiatives cover Digital Platforms, API Security, Email Security, and Attack Surface Management, alongside continuous Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT) to protect digital assets.

nodes.title: Classification and Measurement of Financial Instruments
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Company's classification and measurement of financial instruments into three categories. First, financial assets at amortised cost include bank balances, loans, trade receivables, other receivables, investments, and other financial assets; debt instruments qualify if they have solely payments of principal and interest contractual terms and are held to collect cash flows. Second, debt instruments at FVTOCI require solely payments of principal and interest terms and a business model of both collecting cash flows and selling; gains and losses go to OCI, with impairment, interest, and foreign exchange in profit or loss, and no such instruments exist at reporting date. Equity instruments at FVTOCI are non-trading, non-contingent consideration, irrevocably elected and meeting the equity definition, with OCI amounts not recycled and dividends in profit or loss. Third, financial assets at FVTPL are initially at fair value with transaction costs in profit or loss, subsequently at fair value with gains or losses in profit or loss, including investments held for trading. Financial instruments held for trading are those acquired principally for near-term sale or repurchase, part of a short-term profit-taking portfolio, or derivatives not in qualifying hedge relationships; trading securities are classified as held for trading at FVTPL.

nodes.title: 7.1 Financial instruments Initial recognition (I) Classification of financial instruments
nodes.summary: The section covers the initial recognition and classification of financial instruments, focusing on two key assessments: the business model assessment and the SPPI test. The business model assessment evaluates how the Group manages financial assets at an aggregated portfolio level, considering factors such as performance evaluation, risks, manager compensation, and sales frequency, using reasonably expected scenarios. It also addresses reassessment each reporting period and treatment of changes in cash flows. The SPPI test determines whether contractual cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest, affecting classification and measurement at amortised cost or FVTOCI for debt instruments. The section further details accounting for equity instruments, trading instruments, equity investments, financial liabilities designated at FVTPL, derivatives, hedge accounting (including cash flow hedges), subsequent measurement using the effective interest rate, derecognition due to modification or transfer, and recognition timing.

nodes.title: a) Business model assessment
nodes.summary: The text covers initial recognition and classification of financial instruments, focusing on the business model assessment. Classification depends on contractual cash flow terms and the Group's business model. The business model is assessed at an aggregated portfolio level, not instrument-by-instrument, based on observable factors: performance evaluation and reporting to key management, risks affecting performance and their management, manager compensation (fair value vs. contractual cash flows), and expected frequency, value, and timing of sales. Assessment uses reasonably expected scenarios, excluding worst-case or stress scenarios. Changes in actual cash flows do not alter classification of remaining assets but inform new asset assessments. At initial recognition, the Group determines if new assets fit an existing or new business model. Business models are reassessed each reporting period; no changes were identified in current or prior periods.

nodes.title: Credit Risk: Impairment, Default Definition, and PD Estimation

It outlines the impairment assessment approach, referencing the definition of default and default assessment, PD calculation, exposure at default, loss given default, significant increase in credit risk, and collective ECL assessment. The definition of default specifies 90 days past due and qualitative indicators like emergency funding requests, collateral value decrease, covenant breach, bankruptcy filing, repossession, and restructuring. The PD estimation process uses historical internal data, considers macroeconomic factors, calculates 12-month PD for performing assets, lifetime PD for significant credit risk increase, and 100% PD for credit-impaired assets.
